concept.name: Indirect quotation
concept.definition: An exchange rate quotation expressed from the home country's perspective as the number of units of foreign currency per one unit of home currency. For example, from the euro area's perspective, USD 1.11 = EUR 1.00 is an indirect quotation; the convention is common in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and the euro area.
concept.intuition: Indirect quotation states how much foreign money one unit of your own currency buys.
concept.mechanics: Under indirect quotation the home currency is the unit (base) currency and the foreign currency is the price (quote) currency. It is the reciprocal of the direct quotation, so a rising number under indirect quotation means the home currency is appreciating.
concept.formula: Indirect rate = foreign-currency units per 1 home-currency unit = 1 / (direct rate).
concept.failure_modes: Because the same numerical rate can be 'direct' for one party and 'indirect' for the other, reports that omit the perspective invite sign errors in appreciation/depreciation statements.
concept.misconceptions: Traders sometimes believe one convention is the global standard; in practice both coexist, and only market pair conventions (e.g. EUR/USD, USD/JPY) are standardized, not the direct/indirect label.
concept.example: British newspapers quote cable as USD per GBP (e.g. GBP 1 = USD 1.27); for a UK resident that is an indirect quotation, and a rise to 1.30 means sterling has strengthened.
